content.summary_of_the_paper: The gGN is proposed for the modeling of knowledge representations exploring diagonal + low-rank approximation of covariance using the reverse KL-divergence to quantify node dissimilarity. This is combined in a loss function including three terms, a term promoting first order proximity attracting similar nodes and repelling dissimilar nodes, as well as two additional asymmetric ranking loss terms imposed based on shortest path properties contrasted KL-divergence dissimilarity using a squared error metric. It is demonstrated that the training loss substantially improves when including the low rank approximation as opposed to spherical and diagonal structures only. Furthermore, node properties in terms of shortest path length and node depth are better preserved the more rank components are included and it is further shown by ablations how the three loss components are each important for capturing structure adequately. The approach is further found to well quantify semantic similarity within three genetics datasets constituting directed acyclic graphs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
The approach appears useful with good accuracy characterizing shortest path properties and node depth as well as semantic recovery as quantified using the Davies-Bouldin index.

Weakness
It would be good to contrast performance to forward KL divergence as opposed to the proposed reverse KL-divergence. 

The approach seem to have to ad-hoc tune three objective functions, i.e. the KL term and the two terms characterizing topology of ancesters and descendants. Whereas these three terms are weighted equally it is unclear how in general the three objectives should be combined (weighted in the objective) and such discussion should be included.  The ablation studies are nice, but clearly the impact of the three objectives may differ dependent on the network structure which should be discussed. The loss function including three terms appears presently somewhat ad-hoc.

The validity of the experimental validation is a bit unclear to me. I find it unsurprising that the more complexity is added to the model the more the loss function is reduced (i..e., the loss function can be considered a traning error). Likewise for the experimentation of semantic recovery this also seem to favor complex models accurate accounting for the training data. The authors need to argue why performance is not trivially enhanced by increased complexity and why the results obtained are non-trivial. This is unclear to me at this point.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written and clear in its presentation. Code is made available supporting reproducibility and utility of the approach. The novelty is somewhat limited combining the reverse KL (widely used in other context) with topological constraints imposed using squared error losses. The Use of low-rank approximations are also widely applied including computational merits using Woodbury matrix inversion lemma and Cholesky factorizations. As such, the paper combines well known procedures but in a new context of characterizing directed graph structures.
content.summary_of_the_review: A somewhat incremental paper that improves upon the characterization of DAGs used in semantic characterization of  Biological Process (BP), Cellular Component (CC) and Molecular Function (MF). The paper is well written and clear in its presentation and provides favorable performance when contrasted alternatives. However, it seems the results are essentially demonstrating how the addition of complexity improves upon the characterization and it is unclear how aspects of generalization is quantified as the semantic similarity and recovery of path length and node depth are not executed on test data (please correct me if I am wrong).
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose an approach called gGN to represent nodes of a graph as gaussian distributions. The authors use non-diagonal covariances for the Gaussians, and proposes a loss function that is based on a reverse KL divergence as well as two ranking based components. They demonstrated their work via simulations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

- The proposed approach is to the best of my knowledge original and sufficiently novel. 
- The mathematics for their approach is clearly presented
- The proposed approach is simple and quite natural

- Weaknesses: 

- Their approach, while natural, lacks theoretical backing/justification. The authors provided little justification/guarantees regarding the choices that they have made: why gaussian? how does one pick the rank r in the perturbation? Why the choice of KL rather than other distances between distributions? I agree with the authors in that the choices that they have made are simple and natural, but I would like to see more justification that is rigorous for their choices. 

- Their loss function involves summations with longest shortest paths, and it is not immediately clear how scalable this approach is to larger graphs. 

- the description of their neural network is purely verbal, and the description of their overall loss/objective is scattered across various places, leading to some unclearness in the presentation of their approach. I suggest using a paragraph to provide a unifying description of their overall model in one place.

The paper is written moderately clearly. I have provided suggestions for improvement. 

The idea is natural and to the best of my knowledge sufficiently original.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, the authors propose a novel technique to represent nodes of a graph as Gaussian distributions with non-diagonal covariance matrices. Additionally the authors propose a novel loss function based on reverse KL divergence, which incorporates ranking-based components aimed to asymmetrically preserve the distances between nodes. The authors demonstrate the efficacy of their approach via experimental results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Here below are some strengths of the current work :

1) Being able to model nodes as Gaussian distributions with non-diagonal covariance matrices provides more flexibility to express dependencies between node embedding dimensions. Consequently this should allow to mimic and capture graph based properties compared to alternate modeling techniques using diagonal covariance matrices.

2) The loss function introduced by the authors also incorporates two ranking-based components which can asymmetrically
preserve the distance values between nodes.

Here below are some weaknesses of the current work :

1) The current work needs a stronger motivation and should demonstrate general applicability. We can definitely represent nodes using Gaussian distributions with non-diagonal covariance matrices with rank-k to be able to match graph properties i.e., distances between nodes etc. However there are questions about the approach :

a) Does the method scale to large graphs given the number of parameters required to train the network is R^(n x d x (r+2)) ? Can we use this method using graph containing millions/billions of nodes ? Typically neural networks are parametric methods i.e., they utilize a fixed number of parameters, however this approach seems closer to non-parametric whose complexity is dependent on the input size. 

b) Why is there a need to have R^(n x d x (r+2)) parameters in the network ? Can we not use function approximation techniques to achieve the same goal ? Why is there a need to learn separate Gaussian distribution for all nodes ? How does it help ?

c) As demonstrated in Table 3, the empirical section uses small toy size datasets which raises questions about the ability of the model to scale to larger datasets. 

d) The empirical results seem to have used real-world graph datasets which are from a biological domain. Why did the authors not use datasets from other domains i.e., social and citation networks etc. ? Using datasets from other domains which have strengthened the authors' case in the current work. Otherwise it raises the speculation that biological graph datasets have an inherent bias due to which the authors are able to match distances between nodes etc. 

e) Why did the authors choose to focus their work on directed graphs ? How does the approach work for undirected graphs ?

f) Why do the authors only focus on matching distances between nodes ? How about other properties i.e., diameter, density and sub-graph based values which are important as well ?

g) Why did the authors include only Graph2Gauss as a baseline ? The authors should have included other state-of-the-art approaches to compare against.

2) Some parts of section 3.2 of the work where the authors discuss the loss function are not clear. With regards to equation 3, 
a) Why are the authors pushing node i apart from immediate descendants ? How does it help exactly and what does it achieve ? 
b) Additionally why are the authors reducing the energy between node i and its parents ? 

3) Extending on 1) above, being able to match some graph properties might not be as useful as demonstrating good performance on some downstream inference task. For example, using their approach can the authors demonstrate better node classification and/or edge prediction results compared to state-of-the-art approaches etc. The authors should have included more empirical results from some graph based inference task which would have demonstrated better efficacy of their approach. Additionally have these results would have value to the current work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The current manuscript requires a stronger motivation and/or more empirical results as highlighted above. Some parts of the paper i.e., Section 3.2 are not clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: The current manuscript requires a stronger motivation and/or more empirical results as highlighted earlier.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes to use nondiagonal (diagonal + low-rank outer product) covariance matrices for Gaussian distribution during the node embedding procedure. The overall learning framework shown in this paper is mainly based on two previous works [1] and [2], but with different terms in the training loss function. Simulation results are provided to show the potential benefits of the use of nondiagonal covariance matrices to preserve the graph topology information for downstream tasks.

[1] Vilnis, Luke, and Andrew McCallum. "Word representations via gaussian embedding." ICLR (2015).

[2] Bojchevski, Aleksandar, and Stephan Günnemann. "Deep gaussian embedding of graphs: Unsupervised inductive learning via ranking." ICLR (2018).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The new covariance matrix formulation may have better expressive power with affordable computational complexity than the traditional diagonal matrix. 
2. The new training loss formulation may lead to new theoretical insights about which aspects are important for node embedding.
3. The simulation part covers ablation studies, comparisons with many previous works, and a lot of details. Codes are also provided (via GitHub) for reproducibility.

Weakness:
1. The main concern I have about this paper is the effectiveness of the simulation part. This paper contains a lot of simulation results (not much theory), but they are not that meaningful to me in their current form. All the targets/metrics (e.g., shortest path length, node depth) are directly included in the definition of training loss, so it should be natural for the proposed method to perform well on these aspects, compared to other methods that do not take them into consideration. But this does not mean these aspects are indeed what we need for downstream tasks in practice. In other words, it is not clear how would the new node embeddings work in practice when used by the downstream graph learning models (e.g., graph neural networks) compared to previous methods like [1] and [2]. I would suggest the authors follow at least part of the procedure in [2], where the link prediction and node classification performance are discussed to illustrate the benefits of their method in practice. In this case, one can really see if there is any benefit to using the new training loss/nondiagonal formulation.
2. As the authors have pointed out in the conclusion part, the training procedure requires one to first compute the all-pairs shortest path matrix, which is of complexity $O(n^3)$, where $n$ is the number of nodes in the graph. This is a very time-consuming process, and it is not required by previous methods. I think this is one major drawback of the proposed learning framework w.r.t. computational complexity, but it is not mentioned until the very end (conclusion section). And the existence of GPU implementations for Floyd-Warshall’s algorithms should not be an excuse for not mentioning the complexity earlier, because there also exists parallelization to compute matrix inverse [3] and determinant [4]. If all-pairs shortest paths can be found in parallel, we can also use the entire covariance matrix as a parameter matrix instead of just the low-rank perturbations, which contradicts the first contribution of this paper. I would suggest the authors be fair about the method and move this discussion to the main text, and maybe add a bit more details about how to apply the landmark-based methods to reduce this complexity.
3. Some terms used in the paper are not well-explained and can be misleading. For example, the covariance matrix of the form $\Sigma_i=D_i+P_iP_i^T$ is referred to as a "low-rank covariance matrix" in the main text, while the matrix $\Sigma_i$ itself can be actually full-rank. I understand that it should mean $P_iP_i^T$ is low-rank, but calling $\Sigma_i$ a low-rank matrix can be very confusing in this case. Maybe the authors can have a better name for it. Also, I didn't realize for the simulations the dimension of the "spherical/diagonal" covariance matrix is larger than the "low-rank" covariance matrix until I see Appendix B: "all the embeddings were learned by using latent spaces with the same dimensionality." I think this is important and should be mentioned in the main text as well. Another example is "node depth", the formal definition of node depth appears on page 7 while it is a term used on page 1.
4. This one is minor, but I would like to share it here in case there is any interest. I think the use of forward KL (previous methods) or reverse KL (this paper) really depends on how the directed graph is constructed (i.e., how the directions of edges are determined). From the discussion on page 4, I cannot see the intuition why reverse KL would work better than forward KL. I would suggest the authors add some case studies on some datasets (i.e., WordNet) to elaborate on this part.
5. Some other questions for the authors:
   * What does $S_{ij}^T$ means exactly? Is it just $S_{ji}$?
   * Why do we need $j\neq i$ in Eq. (3)? What if there exist self-loops?
   * In Eq. (5), it should be $E_{ij}/E_{ik}$ or $E_{ji}/E_{ki}$? 
   * Why Eq. (4) and Eq. (5) are claimed to use the ranking information? It seems to me that they are just the sum of MSE in a normalized fashion. Does it make a difference whether we do the normalization or not?
   * When computing $|\Sigma_i|$, the complexity will still depend on $d$ right? According to Appendix A, the complexity should be $O(d+r^3)$ with $r\ll d$, but the dependency on $d$ is ignored on page 4.
   * The title in the pdf seems to not exactly match the one on the website.

[3] Quintana, Enrique S., et al. "A note on parallel matrix inversion." SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing (2001).

[4] Beliakov, Gleb, and Yuri Matiyasevich. "A parallel algorithm for calculation of large determinants with high accuracy for GPUs and MPI clusters." arXiv preprint arXiv:1308.1536 (2013).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper serves as an extension of previous works on representing graph nodes as Gaussian distributions. The authors provide the code for reproducibility. The clarity and quality of this paper can be improved, as some parts of the main text are not well explained. Please see "Strength And Weaknesses" for more details.
content.summary_of_the_review: The ideas and methods proposed in this paper are interesting, but there are still many aspects that are not clear in the current form of this paper. Please see "Strength And Weaknesses" for more details. I would be willing to change my scores if the authors can answer my questions.
